text: What becomes of the mother's income if no daughter is left?
why: A plain question: the will's terms are described, but nothing yet says where the income goes if no daughter is left.

text: Would one daughter's marriage really cripple Dr. Roylott?

text: Would one daughter's marriage really cripple Dr. Roylott? — it would cripple him
why: Holmes states at ¶115 that even one daughter's marriage would cripple Dr. Roylott to a very serious extent.

text: Would one daughter's marriage really cripple Dr. Roylott? — he could live well enough on what was left
id: q.cripple=he could live well enough on what was left
why: An open alternative to Holmes's claim, which the reader can weigh against the remaining £500 in the figures given at ¶115.

text: What reason could anyone have had for wanting Julia dead? — each marriage takes £250 from an income now not more than £750
why: The question presupposes that Julia was killed and that someone wanted her dead, which the story has not established; the coroner found no cause of death.

text: What lies behind the dangers the lady speaks of? — her marriage would take £250 from an income now not more than £750
why: The lady has spoken of dangers at ¶20 and the £250 marriage income and £750 total are stated at ¶115.

text: Why did Dr. Roylott offer no objection to Julia's marriage? — he had the very strongest motives for standing in the way of a marriage
why: The story states at ¶30 that Roylott did not object to Julia's marriage, and at ¶115 that he had strong motives to stand in the way of such a marriage.

text: Why has Dr. Roylott offered no opposition to Helen's marriage? — he has the very strongest motives for standing in the way of a marriage
why: The story states at ¶67 that Roylott has offered no opposition to Helen's match, and at ¶115 that he has strong motives against such marriages.
